purpose: Stage-compatible Hurricane Harvey ledger connecting firm turnover, customer access, resident recovery, and relief judgment while preserving separate analytical units and denominators.

events.geography: United States; Houston, Corpus Christi, and Beaumont MSAs and affected neighborhoods
events.date_precision: Hurricane Harvey landfall and flood period; firm and consumer outcomes are observed through December 2018
events.denominator: Payment-card holders, observed stores, and modeled consumer-demand observations; firm, cardholder, and tract denominators differ and exact counts are not exposed in retained evidence
events.method: Structured extraction from the retained Harvey firm-turnover and consumer-welfare record based on payment-card transactions, store turnover, flood exposure, and a modeled demand panel
events.missingness: No person-level customer identifiers, income, vehicle access, missed purchases, worker outcomes, firm aid or insurance receipt, or individual welfare are retained; modeled surplus is not observed household spending
events.exposure: Flooding was followed by about 1% permanent firm exit and another 3% temporary closure of at least two months in the observed case; major closures were followed by about 15% longer customer travel distance
events.alternatives_before_action: Customers could use surviving stores, same-chain substitution, entrants, other categories, or stop or defer a trip; the retained evidence does not observe each customer's feasible option set
events.immediate_burden_or_benefit: Observed travel distance increased after major closures; average Houston-MSA modeled welfare loss was about 0.29% of pre-storm retail spending, with much larger losses in the most affected tracts
events.choice_or_response: Consumers traveled farther or substituted across stores; entrants contributed more modeled consumer surplus than exiting stores, but entry did not fully replace exits in the hardest-hit neighborhoods
events.person_or_actor_with_control: Firms control opening, closure, and entry decisions within disaster constraints; individual customers control substitution only within their observed or unobserved feasible options
events.remedy_or_institutional_response: The study discusses targeted aid as a modeled policy implication; no firm-level loan, insurance, grant, customer compensation, or verified service-restoration episode is observed
events.immediate_outcome: Firm turnover and customer travel/access changes are observed or estimated at case, store, cardholder, and tract levels
events.protected_outcome: Some customers retained service through surviving stores, same-chain substitution, or entrants; the evidence does not establish equal access or protected household welfare
events.sacrificed_outcome: Some neighborhoods carried additional travel time and localized modeled welfare loss; worker pay, owner recovery, and missed purchases remain unknown
events.cost_risk_transfer: Closure and replacement can shift recovery costs from firms toward customer time, distance, and neighborhood access even when aggregate prices show no durable increase
events.later_outcome: No person-level durable access, household recovery, political judgment, trust, switching, non-use, or exit outcome is retained
events.meaning_and_attribution: No customer or resident attribution, fairness judgment, trust, or identity endpoint is observed in this payment-card study
events.public_or_collective_response: Targeted-aid implications are modeled, not an observed application, receipt, appeal, or collective-action sequence
events.counterexample: Higher-value entrants and small average price effects can coexist with severe tract-level access and time burdens; store closure is not household hardship for every customer
events.source_and_uncertainty: Retained record and finding based on an author-hosted Hurricane Harvey working paper and public abstract; payment-card coverage, merchant selection, modeled demand assumptions, tract exposure, and absent person-level outcomes limit generalization. This event is not a person-level join to the resident survey event.

events.geography: United States; weighted adults in 24 heavily impacted Texas Gulf Coast counties
events.date_precision: Survey fielded late June through late July 2018, approximately 10–11 months after Harvey
events.denominator: Weighted adult resident survey; affected-resident, all-resident, and applicant denominators differ, and exact respondent count is not stated in retained report summary
events.method: Structured extraction from the retained KFF/Episcopal Health Foundation follow-up survey record; survey reports are preserved as descriptive judgments rather than administrative receipt or causal political behavior
events.missingness: No linked damage record, aid approval or payment, amount, delay, denial reason, later voting/contacting/protest, or person-level connection to the firm and payment-card observations is retained
events.exposure: 58% reported property/vehicle damage or a household job, hours, or income loss; among affected residents, 30% remained disrupted and 42% said they were not getting needed help nearly one year later
events.alternatives_before_action: Residents could apply to FEMA/SBA, seek other public or private aid, rely on household resources, or remain without a remedy; the survey does not reveal each resident's feasible alternatives or administrative pathway
events.immediate_burden_or_benefit: Among affected residents, 23% said finances were worse and 17% quality of life was worse; 41% reported a FEMA or SBA application, with reported approval and denial outcomes among applicants
events.choice_or_response: Residents reported applications, recovery judgments, and awareness or lack of awareness of public-input routes; these are reported responses, not verified receipt or observed civic action
events.person_or_actor_with_control: Federal, state, local, and recovery institutions control program design and public-input routes; residents control application and judgment only within information, eligibility, and resource constraints
events.remedy_or_institutional_response: The survey records reported FEMA/SBA application and perceived relief reach; 54% of all residents were confident relief money benefited those most in need, while 42% were not confident
events.immediate_outcome: Recovery progress coexisted with persistent disruption, unmet-help reports, and uneven confidence in relief distribution
events.protected_outcome: A majority reported life largely or almost back to normal and 54% expressed confidence in relief reach; this does not establish recovery or confidence for every affected resident
events.sacrificed_outcome: A substantial affected minority reported continuing disruption, worse finances or quality of life, and insufficient help; durable housing, health, work, and financial security remain unknown
events.cost_risk_transfer: Navigation and uncertainty about relief can leave recovery burden with households even when aggregate recovery appears substantial; the survey does not identify who ultimately absorbs the cost
events.later_outcome: Public-input awareness, trust change, attribution, voting, contacting, protest, relocation, switching, and exit remain open
events.meaning_and_attribution: Relief-confidence and preparedness judgments are reported, but they are not a verified change in institutional trust or political identity
events.public_or_collective_response: The survey measures awareness of long-term federal funding and public-input routes; it does not observe participation or collective action
events.counterexample: A majority saying relief reaches those most in need can coexist with substantial unmet need; aid application is not approval or payment, and confidence is not civic action
events.source_and_uncertainty: Retained record and finding based on the KFF/Episcopal Health Foundation weighted survey; selected-county coverage, self-reported affected status, survey recall, and absence of administrative linkage limit causal and national interpretation. This event is not a person-level join to the firm/customer event.

arrows.to: firm closure and customer travel distance
arrows.evidence: The payment-card case reports firm exit/temporary closure and longer travel after major closures, but the retained record does not link a resident to a particular store
arrows.counterexample: Observed travel change among cardholders does not measure every customer's burden or prove flooding was the only cause of closure
arrows.remaining_gap: Firm-level damage, aid or insurance receipt, customer alternatives, income, vehicle access, and missed purchases

arrows.evidence: The authors estimate average MSA welfare loss around 0.29% of pre-storm retail spending and much larger losses in the most affected tracts
arrows.counterexample: Modeled consumer surplus is not observed household spending, and entrants can raise modeled surplus while failing to restore nearby access
arrows.remaining_gap: Income-specific time cost, affordability, disability, care duties, vehicle access, and stopped or deferred trips

arrows.to: continued resident disruption and unmet help
arrows.evidence: The weighted survey reports 30% of affected residents still disrupted and 42% not getting needed help nearly one year after Harvey
arrows.counterexample: The cross-section cannot establish that disaster exposure caused each reported outcome or identify administrative remedy failure
arrows.remaining_gap: Dated damage, eligibility, application, approval, payment, delay, denial reason, and durable household recovery

arrows.evidence: The survey reports relief confidence and public-input awareness, while later participation, attribution, trust change, and political action are not observed
arrows.counterexample: Relief confidence can reflect general preparedness judgment or information and is not a measure of aid receipt or civic behavior
arrows.remaining_gap: Same-resident administrative linkage, remedy receipt, attribution, trust, public-input participation, voting/contacting, relocation, and exit

boundary: This ledger formalizes a Hurricane Harvey cross-source route from disaster exposure through firm/customer access and resident recovery judgment. It deliberately does not pool payment-card, store, modeled welfare, and weighted survey denominators or claim a person-level causal chain.
storage_boundary: No payment-card panel, survey microdata, raw administrative aid file, or direct identifier is retained; only bounded records, source URLs, denominators, uncertainty, and open arrows are represented.
